analysis.one_liner: Bans firing or refusing to hire workers because of their sexual orientation.
analysis.headline: A bill to outlaw job discrimination against gay, lesbian, and bisexual workers drew 142 cosponsors but never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 1863 would have made it illegal nationwide for employers — including private companies, unions, the federal government, and Congress itself — to fire, refuse to hire, or treat workers differently because they are gay, lesbian, or bisexual, including when the orientation is only perceived. It used the same enforcement system as existing federal race and sex discrimination law, with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission handling complaints. The bill carried major carve-outs: it exempted the armed forces and religious organizations, did not require companies to provide benefits to employees' partners, barred quotas, and let workers claim only outright discrimination, not practices with a lopsided effect. It was referred to four House committees and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Gay, lesbian, and bisexual workers in every state would gain the right to sue when they are fired, passed over, or harassed because of their sexual orientation — including workers targeted because an employer only believes or assumes they are gay, or because of who they associate with. Federal employees and congressional staff would gain the same protection. Workers who are straight but assumed not to be, or who stick up for gay coworkers, would also be protected from retaliation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: LGBT workers with no federal job protection

how_it_helps.text: Makes it illegal for a covered employer to fire, refuse to hire, pay less, or hold back a worker because of sexual orientation, and covers cases where the orientation is only perceived or where the worker is targeted for associating with gay people.

Runs complaints through the same machinery as Title VII of the Civil Rights Act — the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the Attorney General, and the courts — so gay and bisexual workers would get roughly the same remedies as workers facing race or sex discrimination.

Lets workers sue state governments despite constitutional immunity from lawsuits, makes the United States liable for damages just like a private employer, and lets workers who win recover attorney's fees.

Bars retaliation against workers who file complaints or testify, requires employers to post notices of the new rights, and extends coverage to federal workers and congressional employees under the Government Employee Rights Act and the Congressional Accountability Act.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — private companies, employment agencies, labor unions, state and federal governments, and Congress's own employing offices — would bear new legal exposure: lawsuits, settlements, damages, and the cost of posting notices and complying with EEOC rules. Taxpayers would fund the federal government's liability as an employer and the cost of enforcement. Religious organizations and the military were largely written out of the bill, so their costs would be little changed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and governments facing discrimination suits

drawbacks.text: The protections were deliberately narrow: the bill did nothing to require health or other benefits for an employee's partner, barred claims based on a practice's unequal effect (so workers had to prove intentional discrimination), and banned quotas and preferential treatment.

It carved out the armed forces entirely — meaning service members, who could be discharged under the military's ban on openly gay service at the time, got no protection — and exempted religious organizations except their taxable for-profit arms.

Employers and religious-liberty advocates argued the bill would invite costly litigation and force employers to police workplace speech about sexuality; the religious exemption and the ban on disparate-impact claims were concessions to those concerns, but employers would still have faced suits on the Title VII model, which costs money to defend even when the employer prevails.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For gay, lesbian, and bisexual workers, this was the difference between having a federal right to keep their jobs and having none — in 1995, firing someone for being gay was legal under federal law in most of the country. The costs were real but modest and of a kind employers already managed under race and sex discrimination law. The honest critique is about design, not cost: the bill protected against firing but not against benefits discrimination, excluded the very institution (the military) then most aggressively discharging gay people, and offered religious employers a broad exemption. It was a carefully hedged first step, and it never got taken.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees and then three subcommittees, never received a hearing or markup, and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerry Studds of Massachusetts, the first openly gay member of Congress, introduced the bill on June 15, 1995 with a long list of original cosponsors, including Rep. Barney Frank and a bloc of moderate Republicans.

The Speaker referred it to four committees at once — Economic and Educational Opportunities, House Oversight, Government Reform and Oversight, and Judiciary — a split that meant no single committee owned the bill.
Within a month it had been sent down to three subcommittees: Civil Service (June 16), Employer-Employee Relations (June 29), and the Constitution (July 18).

Cosponsorship grew to 142 members — 126 Democrats, 14 Republicans, and 2 independents — roughly a third of the House, but the record shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress.
The bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997; nothing in the action history after the March 1996 introductory remarks suggests it moved again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who preferred no new federal discrimination liability, religious organizations that wanted no coverage, and opponents of federal protections for gay workers were better off — the legal ability to fire someone for being gay continued nationwide. Gay and bisexual workers in the roughly thirty states without state protection remained with no recourse, and the bill had to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers free to keep firing gay workers

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 126 of 142 cosponsors — but 14 Republicans and 2 independents signed on; no vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call split to measure.

industries.industry: Private employers, employment agencies, and labor unions
industries.note: The bill would have given their workers a federal right to sue over sexual-orientation discrimination, adding litigation exposure on the Title VII model. Their freedom to make employment decisions without that liability is the flip side of the protection workers would have gained.

The bill expressly exempted religious organizations from coverage, preserving their legal ability to make employment decisions based on sexual orientation; only their taxable for-profit activities would have been covered.

The military was written out of the bill entirely, leaving in place its policy of the era discharging service members for being gay. Civilian gay workers would have been protected; uniformed personnel would not.

industries.industry: Federal, state, and congressional government employers
industries.note: The bill stripped states of their usual immunity from federal-court lawsuits, made the United States liable for damages like a private employer, and applied the Congressional Accountability Act's procedures to congressional offices — so governments themselves would have faced the same liability as companies.
